blocks.x: I'll make a note here. The date is May 1st, 1961, and we're over at 731 St. Peter Street interviewing Bob Wilbur. Do you mind giving your full name? Do you have any middle initial or name? Robert Sage Wilbur. And do you mind telling just when you were born and where?
I was born March 15th, 1928, in New York City. Can you tell when you first became interested
in music? How old you were and what were the circumstances, if you remember?

Well, I think the first jazz recording I heard was Duke Ellington's Mood Indigo, which my mother or father got when it came out, which was around 1930, I guess, so I was about two or three years old, and I remember it from then. But I became interested in jazz mainly through being interested in the popular bands of the late 30s. And I think the first time that I heard New Orleans jazz was when I bought the album of Louis Armstrong Hot 5 reissues that
came out. About 1940?

About 1940, yeah. And I remember my first impression of this music, the Muskrat Ramble and Yes, I'm in the Barrel and all those wonderful things, it made no sense to me whatsoever. I was used to the big band riffs and there was no, the melodies were much too complex for me to understand. But I stuck with it and got to love the music. And I think that was the reason I became a musician, was Louis Armstrong's not fine.
Yeah, well when did you start and actually, what instrument did you take up first? And when
did you start, about how old? I started playing clarinet when I was 13. 13, yeah.
Yeah. Did you belong to a school orchestra right away or pick it up yourself? What did you do?
No, I studied with the director of the school band, was a clarinet player himself, and I studied with him and started in with the junior band.
You started with the BAME clarinet?
BAME, yeah. Yeah.
And what kind of instrument was it? You know, metal ones or something like that, was it really?

Yeah, I had a Penzlmuller gold clarinet with silver keys and I thought that was much better, much flashier than the wooden ones, you know. Yeah. But I started to try to play jazz even, well maybe two or three years before that with, I had a buddy who was a drummer and I played a little tin flute and we used to play along with records, you know, Bob Crosby and Benny Goodman. A lot of the guys that did down here started on that.
Yeah. Yeah. At that time, who were your favorite musicians? Is that when you actually began playing?

Well, I began playing right as soon as I took up the clarinet and I was very fortunate in the fact that I grew up in Scarsdale. Yeah. That wasn't a fortunate fact, but the fortunate fact was there was a lot of young guys around who were very interested in jazz, who were a couple of years older than I were, who had good collections and they introduced me to all facets of New Orleans, the Chicago players and everything. So I got to know the whole range of the jazz world very quickly.
That group has been written up, I know at times, in the old magazines and all and other wives. Can you tell some of the other fellows that you played with when you started?

Yeah. Well, there was an earlier group that were older than I who have not kept up their professional activities. But the players that were my contemporaries that are still active are Dick Wellstead on piano, who was from Greenwich, Connecticut, and Johnny Glazel, who played trumpet from Scarsdale, and Charlie Traeger was a bass player from Greenwich. He's still playing. Let me see. Jerry Blumberg came in on the scene later. He was from Baltimore.
Jerry was here two weeks ago. He didn't see him.
Yeah. I missed him.
He came about a couple days after he left.

And then Bob Mielke was a trombone player from San Francisco who played with our group and now he leads his own band out there, San Francisco. Eddie Fife was a drummer who played with the original gang and he's working around Washington, D.C. now.
Yeah. I think Jerry talked about it.
Yeah. Yeah.

Can you tell us anything else about your, especially your interest in New Orleans music as it developed in those years? Yeah. Yeah. Also about the whole band, what did you do? Did you play your arrangements just by head or did anybody try to write them out or what did you do?

Well, when we started out playing, the emphasis among the group of musicians around Scarsdale and Westchester was on the Chicago style and the big influence was the music at Nick's, which was the place in New York.
Did you all get down there? I don't remember now the policy of letting kids in under age or not. What did they do?

I don't remember. I remember when I was 13 and mostly on Sunday afternoons and they would let, they had, at that time they had a dance floor and they had three pianos lined up, three upright pianos in front of the bandstand. I remember that, yeah. And they used to let us kids sit inside the piano and actually sit on the edge of the bandstand. And I'd be sitting there like two feet from Brad Gowan's feet and peewee. And I think Chelsea Qualey was on trumpet at that time and sometimes Hackett. So that was, they were very nice about letting kids in, you know, because they knew we were young musicians, you know, and wanted to learn. In fact, I remember, I guess I was 14 or 15, going into places on 52nd Street and they didn't bother me. By yourself? Your parents? Anybody take care of them?
No, no, no.

Kids, it seems amazing now, but I remember a thrilling time going into Kelly's stables and sitting at a front table, right in front of the bandstand. And the band was playing and Coleman Hawkins walks up to the bandstand and picks up the tenor and one of the fellows in the band says, what do you want to play, Hawk? And he says, body, one, two. And he starts playing. And they didn't bother us.
Any other places you remember hearing in those days around New York? I was there off and on all through those years too.
Yeah.
I don't remember all the places either anymore.

Well, there was George's Tavern in the village where Frankie Newton used to play and Al Casey, guitar player, played there. The village vanguard used to have nice groups like Art Hodes had a trio there with Max Kaminsky and Freddie Moore.
I remember, I think, Albert Nicholas and Zutti and others were there. Yeah. Lead Belly quite a while.

Yeah. Yeah. Well, I remember, I guess this was 1940 or 41, hearing the wonderful group that Teddy Wilson had at Cafe Society with Edmund Hall and Sid Catlett and Emmett Berry and Benny Morton, who I've been working with recently. Yeah, I remember that group too. Yeah.
And had a Cafe Uptown one too. They had two of them going.
Yeah. Cafe Society Uptown and Downtown too, yeah. Yeah. Uh, I'm trying to think, the first time I heard Sidney Bechet was...
Yeah, I was going to ask if you can remember.
Yeah. I think that the first, the first record I heard of his was, uh, Rose Room and Lady Be Good.
Yeah, the Victor ones.

Yeah. And I, I picked it up, picked him up because I liked the tunes. I didn't know anything about Sidney Bechet at all. Yeah. And, uh, that was my first contact with him. I got more and more interested in his playing.
When did you first hear him in person? Can you remember that?

Yeah, the first time I heard him in person was at a swing soiree that was called, it was held at a place called the Pied Piper in Greenwich Village. I remember that. Which, uh, in recent years was called the Cafe Bohemia. They used to have a lot of modern jazz groups there. It was on Barrow Street. And, uh, Wilbur de Paris ran some sessions there. And this particular one he had Sidney and, uh, Bill Coleman on trumpet and Mary Lou Williams. It was, that was the first time I heard Sidney in person. It was thrilling. I got to meet him. And, uh, I really got to get together with Sidney on the, uh, studying with him through Mesmesro, who I'd known. I met him when he was playing at Ryan's. With Art Hodes. Art had a trio with Mez and Danny Alvin on drums. And that was, that was the first place I ever got a chance to sit in with professional musicians, you know. Because Mez let me sit in. And, uh, Mez had formed the King Jazz Record Company at that time. Yeah. And was just starting to record Sidney with Sidney. And, uh, through him I learned that, that Sidney was opening up a school, a school of music.
Well, I never really knew anything about that school. Oh yeah. Did he really, was it gonna be a real school?

He was gonna settle down and teach because, uh, there wasn't that much playing going on. He just, he wasn't, uh, it seems surprising now in the light of his tremendous popularity in France in later years. But, uh, he couldn't get, uh, bookings, you know. He wasn't a draw, particularly.
So I remember back in 1939 when he was, had a pressing shop up there. Yeah. It was out of music altogether.
Right.
We'd go up there and eat and take some food. I remember once we took a bag of sweet potatoes and Fred Ramsey and I went up to see him one night. Yeah. He was really down and out practically.
Yeah.
A few years before that and he started working at Nick's about that time too.
That's right, yeah.
The Spirits of Rhythm and that group. Yeah.
Zutty and, uh, yeah.
Yeah, Zutty. And he and Zutty didn't get along and then they had to decide, ride up the band somehow.
Yeah. Well, the, uh, I went to see Sydney in, uh, for my first lesson. It was, uh, spring of 1946. I'd been out of high school since a year before. And, uh.

You didn't have any lessons before that time. I was thinking you had. No, no. Cause I remember when Bunk's band was in New York in the fall of 45, you all were playing there. Some of the fellows would go up there to hear the group. Yeah, that's right.
The Starsville. Yeah, that's right. I remember. Uh, that's right. And at that time I was up at Eastman School of Music in Rochester.
Well, I remember Johnny used to come there to hear the band at the Stuyvesant in the fall of 45. Yeah. You weren't there then.

I was at school in Eastman and, uh, and hated to be away because I was more interested in Bunk playing at the Stuyvesant on 52nd Street. Yeah. Than being up at Eastman studying the classics. Yeah. So I just stayed one term.
How old were you then about?

I was, uh, 17. 17 then, 45. Yeah. 45, yeah. Uh, what was the 8th? Did you finish high school? Yeah, I finished 18, uh, I finished high school the spring of 45 and this was the following fall. Yeah. So, uh, after Christmas I gave up Eastman and came back and told my folks I wanted to study jazz at the Stuyvesant Casino on 52nd Street. And that's, that's what I did.
Yeah. So you started with Sidney then in 46.
Yeah, in the spring of 46. Yeah, in the spring of 46. And he, he had this old ramshackle house in Brooklyn on Quincy Street. Yeah, I never did get over there.
I knew about it though. Yeah.

I never seen it. And, uh, uh, he had a sign up front that he made that said Sidney Bichet School of Music. Yeah, I don't remember that. And it was, I know, I like, I think he liked the house and bought it because it, it had these old French New Orleans style windows in it.
By the way, was he living with an Indian girl? Seems like I heard it that time.
Yeah, an Indian girl named Laura. Laura, yeah. From Canada, yeah. Yeah. And he had a beautiful big Great Dane puppy named Butch. Never saw that.
Yeah.
And so I, I came over and, and, uh, bought my clarinet and played for him. And I guess he, he was really pleased at the start because I obviously was trying to play like he, you know, he was my idol.
What kind of clarinet did you have in those days?

By then I'd graduated to a wooden clarinet, uh, BAME. I don't remember what make it was. Yeah. So, uh, then I started taking lessons once a week from him. And it was, they were supposed to be our lessons, but they always lasted much longer. Yeah.
How much did he charge for the way?
I think it was $5 a lesson. That's a pretty good price.
Sure. Really? On those days.
And he got, he got very interested and excited about teaching. I was the only student in the school. I mean. Oh really? Yeah. You mean he didn't? That was all I was.
Really? Yeah.
Yet he was trying to make a go of it, huh? Well, he never had a really kind of realistic picture of it, you know.
No, I guess not. No, he shouldn't.
But, uh, he was very interested in, in trying to teach somebody his idea of improvisation, you know.
Mm-hmm.

And, uh, the way he would go about teaching was, would take a melody and, and, uh, give me an idea of how to phrase it and play the melody straight. The first chorus to show, to, to give the people a melody. And then, uh, he showed me how to work out variations on the melody, which was his, the basic idea of his playing was variations on the melody, not just, uh, over a series of progressions, you know. Yeah.
Well, actually, uh, tried to keep the melody going in some sort of a form.
Yeah, yeah.
Uh, did he first demonstrate it for you, if you take up a new number? For instance, what pieces did you remember playing?
Well, I remember, uh, Rockin' Share, who worked on that.
Yeah.
And, uh, one of the pieces that he worked on, he never recorded it, but he had a very elaborate set of variations on it, was intermezzo, in which he would play for the first chorus.
You know, the, violin number, in, uh, from a movie, or?
From the movie, the Leslie Howard, uh, movie, yeah. Dun, Oh, yeah.
Yeah, Tasha saw it, though, and played it in the movie, and then he did it.

Yeah. And he, the first chorus, where you play the melody, and the second chorus was variations in double time against the melody. And then, uh, oh, another tune we worked on was that, uh, Prisoner of Love, which was popular at the time, you know. And his idea was, you have to take the, take the, uh, melodies that the people want to hear, the popular, the popular tunes, and, uh, play the melody, and then play variations on it, but, you have to have the relationship between the variation and the melody clear, you know.
Yeah.

And he was, uh, he never thought of New Orleans jazz as being something of the past that he was recreating. He was always, Yeah, like Tiger Rag, and he didn't worry about those standards. He was always thinking in terms of contemporary, uh, in a contemporary expression. It was like when Bunk took his band to Stuyvesant. Yeah.

casino he wanted to play bell-bottom trousers and white Christmas and things like that and all these jazz fans they wanted to hear old New Orleans tunes you know he didn't care about that. Saints and all that. Yeah yeah and also was Sydney always made the point that in New Orleans they had to play for many different kinds of people and they had to know all kinds of music they played for Irish people they played Irish music and and waltzes and everything. You didn't even discuss
those things with you. Yeah sure. I started to ask again the procedure in the lesson if you'd start say with a new number like Rockin' Shabbard he played over for you first or did you know it pretty

well and have you play it right off or what did he do? Well I would I would know the melody pretty well but he would he would start playing it and and have me play a harmony part or accompaniment to it along with it. And then if I did something that was wrong or not good he would show me how to do it
you know. By the way was he using his soprano sax all the time there did he ever play clarinet? No he

used played the clarinet a lot. He played the clarinet in those days. He loved to play the clarinet except on a job he was always a little afraid of it because he couldn't express himself as freely on the clarinet it was a little more delicate you know but at home he loved to sit and play the clarinet.
Oh do you remember anything about his clarinet? I know he gave one of them once when he sort of gave up he had trouble with his teeth he gave one to John Reed's wife you knew John Reed I
suppose had been connected. Yes I know I knew of him I never met him yeah. Remember that was 1943

I visited them in Cincinnati after he left victory went to Crosley during the war and shortly before that he'd become discouraged with the clarinet on account of his teeth or something and decided to give it up if I remember it was 1943 there. Yeah. And he gave her one of his old clarinets and then later he had his brother to fix up his teeth and some bridge work. Do you know anything about his teeth? Did you ever inspect them or did he ever talk about them? No. Did he show you anything? No. Never did no. They didn't seem to be giving him any trouble at that time. I think he maybe had a bridge or something. Yeah. His brother spent a lot of time in trouble fixing it up. I think he did yeah. I don't know just what he did.
But he was a marvelous clarinet player I think if he had stuck with the clarinet he would have

perhaps been the greatest. You know all the old-timers like Bunk once said he was the greatest and yeah around New Orleans he was like. Yeah around here they talk about even in Chicago there's one little story I'll tell you briefly Natty Dominic tells about when Johnny Dodds and Natty were playing at the Gallows 29 Club that would be in the late 30s even. Yeah. Evidently Sidney was with Noble Sissel. Noble Sissel yeah. And he came to town once Jimmy Noon happened to come in sitting at a table had his instrument and Sidney walked in. Yeah. Johnny said uh-oh here comes the devil uh-oh he untow my playhouse. Yeah. Well Sidney said that he one of his he made his big

reputation around New Orleans in the early days one of the things was that he never played a clarinet and when they played those rags in the Red Book they were written in in keys. Yeah mostly of them sharp keys. The players would would play like sharp keys six sharp something like that.
The thing for the violin is really the lead instrument in that band. Yeah. And all the
players would have eight clarinets to play on. Well Sidney would play these parts on on a B flat

clarinet and that was quite a feat you know. Well anyway Sidney said well I see you all got your sticks with you come on get them out let's get up meaning uh Jimmy Noon because Dodds was already up there. Yeah. Yeah. So all three of them played at once and Natty said you know who was left when they all got through? Sidney. Yeah. He chased Johnny and and Jimmy Noon. Yeah. I'll believe it because Sidney had the
the fastest uh articulation and tonguing of of uh any player I've heard. Oh another little story I'll

put on here since we don't have in our two lane uh archive either at uh once when Mary Carolli who liked uh Johnny Dodds very much as well as Sidney Bouchet and Jimmy Noon too she knew all three was clarinetists and um when she was visiting Jimmy Noon and he said you know uh Johnny Dodds thinks he's the greatest clarinetist in the world but uh you know he isn't he really isn't and uh so Mary said who is he thought maybe Jimmy would say well I am but yeah Sidney Bouchet. Yeah. No doubt about it all Sidney Bouchet is the greatest. Sure. And yet it doesn't his playing doesn't show up he doesn't play enough clarinet on different records that we can really tell that he was that sensational because there must have been some awfully good clarinetists down here too like the Teos and others. Oh yeah. And yet a lot of the old timers say Sidney was the best. Well I think I think his playing on the uh the things
he did for Panacier around 1938. Yeah those. Uh weary blues and Giada and those I think those are the best

examples on record of his clarinet. Another funny little story Steve Smith once uh who had been recording Sidney well a little bit later actually about almost that same time but he liked Sidney a lot too. He had the Hot Record Society and reissues and later put out some on his own label and he happened to be going um in the elevator. I thought those were all on the first floor but I think it was in the elevator. It must have been on the second floor someplace on 23rd street and Sidney was saying before the one of those sessions he said when Mez hears these records he's going to think this clarinet sounds awfully good. It's not going to be it's not going to be Mez's clarinet it's going to be mine on there that he's hearing it. As if Mez didn't have sense enough you know to know his own clarinet when he heard it. But Sidney was saying that he was going to be the star of that session and all. He had that in mind. But yeah as you say that was very good on some of those. Yeah excellent. And the soprano saxon they're really the blues and those things were very very good too. Oh brilliant yeah. Yeah. Anything else about his clarinet that impressed you? You think he got around on it faster and all around at the lessons too not so much afraid that he might miss something or you mean that? If he had

played it more he would have been you know the speed would have been phenomenal. Yeah. Because he had the natural technique on it but a clarinet you just have to play all the time. You can pick up a saxophone after a few days and not playing and it's not as delicate a thing you know. Yeah it seems to be much easier to control the read and the fingers too. And Sidney always had a feeling that he had to carry a
band you know. Yeah you get that very much from hearing it in person as well as his record. Well to some
extent it was his own fault because uh he he would often hire inferior players and then be mad at them

for not playing up to his standards you know. But you think he maybe did that so he'd stand out and be the star? He liked the limelight as they say? He did like that yeah. I thought he did too but I don't know I wonder.

Uh with the clarinet he couldn't get the power that he wanted and this is part of his part of his expression but there was a this this wonderful gentle side to his nature that came out in his music and and it really came out in the clarinet because he played the most uh marvelously tender gentle way

yeah um Jimmy Noonbladen an improved albert and yeah I think Johnny Dodds had more keys than usual the the some of the players around here even like like the old 13 key which yeah well I think the

albert and maybe I like their tone and no it's it's got a very uh dark quality to the sound it's the only word I can think of and a lot of uh wood the sound of wood and the modern clarinets they make today uh are getting completely away from that type of sound they're getting more of a brilliant trumpet like sound so the kind of clarinet i play is a an old selmer bt selmer which is about 30 years old which was a large bore the largest the difference in the bore maybe and the albert system had always had a large bore and that seems to give you that tone quality the uh the reason they're making the smaller bore today is because of intonation you can get more precise intonation with a smaller bore but with a large bore you have a greater flexibility and you can get all uh you can vary the tone and and get all different kinds of timbers and glissandos and everything all those effects that that dodds and and bichet used you couldn't do on a modern clarinet it's just too inflexible the instrument is too

inflexible yeah i wonder if other players will tell us that they don't even can't even tell the difference some of the fellows here that play um albert they'll say well they could never tell the difference they just picked it up because it's the cheapest thing they could get maybe but i always thought myself maybe there's really a difference yeah i think there is because of the larger bore incidentally i'll put this little story on too i don't want to take up all the time talking but we don't have this up there either a friend of mine armand van der heit in chicago was an amateur clarinetist and learning um working pretty hard at it and learned to play jazz fairly good he was didn't start until maybe he was 25 or something and he studied with one of the chicago symphony man yeah and uh this fellow had him using a real hard reed finally about a number five reed or something and a different embouchure so he made so much noise squeaking and working on real high notes at home that his neighbors wouldn't stand for it he'd come down to our place where john steiner and i had a big place above a shock absorber factory and he could play all night he'd come over there and practice at night yeah because he worked in the daytime and uh and on this new embouchure it sounded terrible squeaking and squealing and up on his high notes yeah it was a hard reed and he told his finally said his teacher told him that if he worked on this new embouchure and developed it right he'd developed the tone of an albert clarinet and i couldn't hardly believe it because i used to kid him and tell him why don't you throw that beam away and buy one of the old ten dollar alberts that we had around yeah yeah but it's the symphony man that appreciated that had a different tone too and i could hardly believe that they would recognize it yeah but have you uh amongst other clarinetists do you think um they would admit that or not that there's a difference in the tone

Yeah, he always said, practice, but when you get tired, stop. You know, don't keep practicing if you get too tired.
We were talking about practicing. Do you think Sidney ever practiced much at home or what did he ever do by himself?

Yeah, he used to play a lot and he had a tape machine. By that time, he had one of these brush sound mirrors that had come out around 1948. And they were a very good machine. They were kind of difficult to operate by today's standards.
The first one out, yeah. Yeah.

But he had a lot of fun with that and he used to play the soprano with a tape machine on and listen to it back and everything. And also at that time, he was very busy composing tunes and also working on this...
That opera or ballet, I guess you might.
Ballet, yeah, which later was produced. This was when he was really working on it.

I remember 1944, I was once up in Harlem with John Reed to see him in the basement apartment where he had a piano and he got out the score and played it. He played not too well on piano, actually, as you know, I guess.

He loved to sit at the piano and play. And he had his own distinctive harmonic idiom in his tunes. It was limited, but he had certain progressions which were unusual that you could identify with Sidney. They say, yeah, that's one of Sidney's progressions.
Yeah.
You know.
Oh, by the way, did you ever hear that record? It was on a 10-inch London and I never... It was cut out before I got in the record business down here.
Yeah, the classical record made in Paris. In Paris, yeah. Yeah, I did. In fact, I heard it before it came out because Sidney came over here in the early 50s with the test pressings on it.
You know of anybody that owns it? Many people around New York have it or anybody... You don't own it, I guess.
I meant to pick it up.
We should have all bought one.
I know, I know.
It's too bad.

The music is very interesting. It's very much Sidney. He was tremendously influenced by late 19th century romantic music. And it sounds like Chopin and that type of thing. Then the blues comes in, you know.

I never got much of an impression, you know, from him playing it. Maybe for five minutes he picked out parts of it to show us. And he was struggling a good deal with the piano. By the way, do you remember, did he play on it himself? Yes, he did. I got the idea that he was soloist, special soloist.
He was soloist on it, yeah.
With the Reggae Symphony, wasn't he?
Yeah, that's right.
That's the impression I got, but I never did hear it and I wasn't sure if that was right.

I think his early experience when he was, what, 19 years old, of playing in Europe with the Will Marion Cook band and as a soloist in front of what to him was a real concert orchestra made a tremendous impression on him. And all during his later life, that was sort of an ideal to be a great soloist before a huge orchestra, you know. Yeah. And Will Marion Cook was one of his idols in a sense.
He did talk about it.

Yeah, he used to talk about it a lot. And he talks about it in his book about Will Marion Cook's music. And I'm kind of interested in looking up this music and seeing what it is. You know, I don't know too much about his music.
I have a few pieces I've picked up, but nothing that looks, you know, anything exceptional or more popular tunes.
Sidney always raved about his music, said the marvelous things that he wrote.
I'll check on some of it. I've never really looked at it. I pick up the stuff and don't take time to study.
Yeah.

Do you remember anything else he talked about? At your lessons, did he do much talking? Did he ever get in the talkative mood and start talking about the old history or anything of the music back here? Not that I expect you to recite all of it, but I just wondered how much interested he was in the past down here. Was he trying to get away from it? What do you think? He never did come back here very much. He came back once during the war and made some records.
Yeah. Not too much, no. No, he was interested in music of the day that he was playing.
Something he was living, yeah, sure.
I remember one piece that he taught me was Raggin' the Scale, which was an old... What was that?
Claypool or something? Claypole or something, I think.
Yeah, it went... That was an old Raggin'. I remember that. He taught me this because now you get a chance to practice your scales, but you can swing them too, you know.

Did he advise you to keep on practicing scales or anything like long notes? Did he ever give you any technical advice on what to practice at home? Of course, he knew that you'd had all of the other instruction, I guess.
No, his principal thing was to practice the idea of making variations on tunes and phrasing and rhythm and getting the idea of swinging, you know.
In regard to counting, did he advise you to pat your foot or did he ever give any advice on that?
Well, yeah, but he used to pat his foot when he played.

Yeah, I remember that. Some people say it's very bad and other, most of the better musicians that are down here did actually pat their foot in public as well as when they practiced. It's one of the almost principles they learned by.

Well, he carried a rhythm section around in his head and, you know, he says, don't rely on anybody around you in playing, you know. Just hear your own rhythm up there and swing against that, you know.
By the way, are you watching the time? Yeah.
Oh, I'm sorry, I've got plenty of time.
It's now, the time is at 6.30. 6.30, yeah. I mean, there's any time you have to quit and don't let me get interested and forget.
Sidney had this talent of being able to play in any company and making some music somehow. And some of those bands that he had to play with in France in the later years were really atrocious.
I thought so too. But he would make them play, you know.
He always made any group he played with sound better with him than without him. You know, he brought out the best in players.

I remember hearing him once up in his apartment where he'd just play by himself. And, you see, at that time he was, oh, he'd just gotten back from the section there in memory of Johnny Dodds. That tune I never cared anything for. For you, Johnny. Oh, yeah. Blues for you, Johnny.
All too sentimental, the tune.

Yeah. In fact, he gave me his original manuscript. I'm not sure that he wrote it out. It might have been somebody else that helped him with it. By the way, let's get on to that. Did you ever see him read music very much? The only time I really saw him was reading the piano score to this.
No, no. He never was a good reader.
I didn't think so.
No, no.
Did he advise you that it was good to read or bad to read? Or did he give you any... Oh, yeah.
He felt bad that he couldn't read better than he did, you know. He advised me to work on the reading, you know.
Yeah. Mm-hmm.
Yeah.
Didn't seem to hurt his playing any.

But he showed me all his... He had choruses of variations worked out on certain tunes that he would always play when he played the tunes. They were his specialties, like China Boy, I Know That You Know, The Sheik of Arabi, which he had a whole chorus of variations, which he recorded on the one-man band record.
Oh, yeah.
But he recorded on tenor, and it didn't sound as effective as when he played it on soprano.
Mm-hmm.
And he showed me all these...
Yeah, come in. See, we were talking about Sidney's variations. He had these certain standard choruses.
Yeah.
Did he ever talk anything about that one-man band record that you mentioned?
Well, I remember he said Sidney had a horrible toothache when he was making it, and he just wanted to get it over with and get out. I thought it was quite a feat. Yeah. Quite a wonderful thing.
Pretty good.
But we used to... As I got to play better on the soprano, I was working on the soprano by now, too.
Oh, yeah.
Yeah. And I began to... He went into Ryan's with a little group with Lloyd Phillips on piano and Freddie Moore on drums.
Yeah.

And I started playing with him there. And we did... I know that you know these variations in unison, the two sopranos, and we did China Boy in unison, the two sopranos, and all these things. It was quite an effect, and we never recorded it. I wish we had.

I think we have that record. I mean, it'd be good to get your recollections of that record. If I can find it, the one that you made with Sidney. It was right over here the other day. You can start talking about it now if you've done it.
Well, I made two records with Sidney. One was the Columbia...
Oh, the Columbia album.
Yeah. With the Wildcats. And then I made one for Circle with him of his own tunes with the band I had at the time.
Can you tell us whose idea it was and all, and anything that you can tell us at all about this?

Well, Sidney got this date for Columbia through Georgia Vacian. And he used our band, my band, in order to give me a break, you know, get a chance to record, which was very nice. Because we were just not... We were two inexperienced players to really play up to his level, and when you hear the record, you hear it. You know, we're just... He's carrying the load on his back. But I got a chance to try my hand at writing, and those were my first, really, arrangements I did for that album.
Oh, let's see. Did those all come out? I forget now. This album... Did these come out in the album form first?
Yes, they did, yeah. Half the album is with our group, and the other half was with a corset.
I didn't know some of those would come out singly. Because one of those was never reissued on the long play. Do you remember if there are any of the long play ones?
I haven't seen the long playing version.

There's one of those left out. I forget which one. Right now, I mean, I have to think of it again. What would be your favorite Sidney Bechet records if you had to pick two or three? Either clarinet or soprano, or any group, any time in his life. All the way back to those old Clarence Williams.
Yeah. One of my favorites would be Cakewalkin' Babies.
Yeah, sure. One of my favorite records of all time. Which one, the OK or the Jeanette?
They're both great, but I think I would give the edge to the one with the... One has a team singing on it. A man and a woman, I think.
I think that's the Jeanette, yeah.
And the other one has a girl singing.
Yeah, the Steve of Taylor.
That one is the one that I think is best. I think that's a fantastic record.
I think that's the... record. The OK, then, yeah. They're a little better recorded, too.
And Sidney's playing is just fantastic at that young age. Virtuosity was unbelievable on the instrument. Just as great as it ever was later.
Yeah, I think so.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And another favorite of mine for... Just to show his pure lyrical playing of a melody was that Indian summer he made in the late 30s.
Oh, yeah. Yeah. On Bluebird.
Yeah. And then the things that he made for Victor, the first New Orleans feet warmers and things like Mankley Frag and Shag and Lay Your Rocket.
Yeah. Yeah. Really lively, noisy things, but they grow, don't they?
Yeah. They sure do.
By the way, Sidney, I think, told somebody in my presence even once that his favorite record of his own of all times was the Lady Luck.
Lady Luck to blues.
Lady Luck blues. He made that with Mamie Smith, who was a second-rate singer for my money, but still, I guess, might have been pretty good if you'd hear it in person.
I heard that record once. Oh, this was around 1940. I've never heard it since.

It plays a real nice chorus in the middle of it in the back of her. I don't know that I'd ever pick it as my favorite, but I think it's interesting that he might have changed his mind the next day and told somebody else something else, too, but at least that was what he told somebody. I'm pretty sure I heard him say that.
Yeah.
Any other of his favorites that you think are extra good examples of his work?
I always liked the clarinet chorus that he took on a noble sizzle record of I'm Just Wild About Harry.
For real. I don't remember that. That was Decca, I guess, was it?
Decca or Brunswick. I've been trying to pick up that record for a long time.
Careless Love. He did Careless. Some of those same numbers he did on both labels. Yeah.
And another record that he plays magnificent, more or less, within the ensemble is, oh, now what's the name of that thing? Swing Parade.
Wait a minute. I can't think of it now.

It was a thing. It started out with the first part of Marilyn by Marilyn. And then it went into another March melody, which was more characteristically Sydney. Yeah. I remember. And Sydney plays just, and the band is not that good. In fact, he played great on that whole session, Sleepy Time Down South. It takes a beautiful chorus. I can't give anybody none of my jelly rollers on that session.
Yeah. I remember that. Sydney.

Paris yeah I like to I think I liked his playing best in that period I liked it better than the playing in his later years where his tone got a little deeper and not quite as he didn't have as much finesse later than as he did then I thought his playing was great in those Victor records the tone was very clear later his tone got a little more of a gruffness heaviness to it well by the
way I said that same day that he played the blues for you Johnny and gave me that manuscript he played this famous tenor aria from Pagliacci yeah you know I guess

he never recorded that did he yeah he loved to play that thing any any he interpolated it into a dear old Southland yeah that's how he would use it thing all the way through though that day I remember playing a concert with Sydney at Colgate University with the Wildcats and and him as a featured soloist and just he just broke up the house with that Pagliacci and these are just college kids college boys and they just he just bowled them over yeah another thing that he played great a favorite tune of his that I don't think he ever he did record it for
Columbia but they never issued it was a song of songs and he would play it ad lib out of tempo

he said that this is one of the songs here this oh they did they came out later they didn't put it in the original album but they put it in there they dropped some of the stuff out of this album and added some more oh yeah and my woman's blues too that was another great thing there might be something on there of yours a second master that's what I was interested to find out if there's anything second masters on there if you remember you're not so familiar with the long play then
no I don't know this long playing but I remember him recording all these things but some of them Song of Songs wasn't released on the original album and neither was My Woman's Blues

is there anything you can tell us about how you all organized those sessions and worked out the different second parts some of them started the remembrance from the time you had your lessons and that you worked together do you think well this was I was still studying with Sidney at the time we made the records and living with him in Brooklyn you were living over there oh yeah well you didn't tell that oh yeah I moved in finally

oh gee I didn't know that see I had been living in New York and and we were having sporadic jobs with the wildcats around town but there were not that many jobs and I was having trouble meeting my 10 or 12 dollars a week rent on my room you know so Sidney said oh that's all right man you come in and move in with me here you know didn't even charge your rent you know no no rent or anything and I took over the front room where he had been giving his lessons and slept on the couch there and and Sidney lived down the basement with Laura and Butch the dog and then he had a couple of few tenants upstairs that helped pay expenses you know yeah so I lived there oh I must have been in the
remember the name of the street and the address and all?

Quincy Street I can't remember the exact address yeah so at that time I was living there I remember we had we had a couple of rehearsals and all the guys in the wildcats came over to Sidney's house and we rehearsed there in the front room and he would show each player what to do at you know at a certain spot yeah he was showing at the piano or demonstrate on his horn you know and then I wrote out some little arrangements backgrounds for the guys
so you had everything organized then over there for the session you didn't have to worry about getting in the studio and figuring out something to do

yeah oh we had to organize it because we were all scared stiff you know we had actually recorded before we made a two things for well no we did two things for uh Commodore records oh yeah I remember that and that was let me see that was uh in uh March or April of that year and these were made in August but that Commodore session it took us about five hours to make four tunes yeah because uh not used to being in a recording studio very nervous you know uh let me see what else
well I was gonna ask which subway station how far over in Brooklyn was that

well I used to go to Hoyt and Skimmerhorn and then change to the GG train and get off at I think it was Franklin and Ostrand avenues over quite a little ways yeah yeah I never did know just where it was I never
did he buy that property or yeah he owned this house yeah
he probably lost it later he reminds me

at that time we once went up to Harlem to see him when he was living in a basement with John Reed and he knew John was somewhat of a better businessman than he was that's when he was playing the opera for us yeah and he'd just bought a summer place over in New Jersey probably in the swamp lands you know like in the near the Hackensack River some real dump where nobody would ever have wanted to build but he bought a place over there right along one of those awful rivers that wasn't any good at all yeah and John was trying to tell him politely you know he shouldn't have done it yeah yeah and I know other times he'd spend all of his money on cameras and equipment oh yeah cars and everything else
and he had a mink farm
well I think I remember something I heard about that
was it in the Mohawk Valley someplace up there yeah and he was going to go up to try to raise mink well that never worked out either no he wasn't much of a businessman
I guess he had a lot of fun in his life though
oh yeah sure
when was the last time you saw him

last time I saw Sidney was I guess it was 1952 or 53 and he came over this country and did a tour uh... and uh... I was in the army at the time and uh... my wife was working at as a cashier at a movie theater on the east side and she's in her booth there one day and Sidney walks up and says hi here I am well my wife had known Sidney before I even knew her in fact I met her she used to go into Ryan's to listen to Sidney and uh... and he had just gotten a letter from France from his mistress informing him that he was about to be a father and he was I mean going not about to be but going to be a father and he was uh... very excited about being a father but worried about his wife's reaction to all this you know but somehow apparently he worked it out alright because for years there he had two homes maintained two homes one for his wife and one for his mistress and uh... boy little boy Daniel

reminds me about the same time as when I saw Sidney last in Chicago about 1952 and uh... he was playing at uh... the old blue note I guess before they moved and uh... he was staying down at the south side hotel he'd had trouble with Ruth Reinhardt he'd left there unexpected suddenly you know without uh... uh... completing his contract and she was always going to sue him and he's always having a lot of bad luck in any case it's partly his fault remember he told that day that he'd... Ruth had been after him he was going to sue him again and uh... also he answered the door at his hotel and the woman comes to the door and he opens the door and she puts the baby in his arms and says here this is your baby that's all and she walks away he doesn't remember ever seeing that woman probably wasn't his baby at all
you know

it's just one of those things somebody taking advantage of him in that particular case so he had to get rid of the baby somehow but all those things were taking up his time and worrying him yet he played wonderfully at night yeah sure big chief Russell Moore was in the band I forget who else now yeah just about a four piece group that he was featured entirely no trumpet
well he had always had trouble with his stomach yeah that's right
and it was always giving him pain yeah that's right he was taking medicine in those days too

he would take this chalk medicine and uh... I remember at that time Rudy Blesch had a Saturday afternoon show and he used to play the show and sometimes his stomach would be acting up and he'd feel horrible but he'd go over and you'd never know it from the playing

I invited him out to dinner that time he went to a Chinese restaurant and he was talking about different ways to cook gumbo about three different kinds of gumbo yeah he also explained how he was trying to get his stomach coated with this medicine yeah
yeah
yeah he was always having a lot of troubles that was the last time you saw him did you ever get to Paris did you ever hear him over there?
no I never did no I was in England in 56 but I didn't get over and he was in Italy at the time touring he wasn't in Paris

I see your friend it's been so long since I've seen him Robert Lewis is that his name? Robert Lewis Robert Lewis yeah he sent him a soprano sax there that's right a year or so before he died he came through here and we had a nice little interview with him he took a few lessons from him
that's right
not as extensively as you yeah gave us some nice ideas of Sidney's latest days sure you'd seen him over there
I wish I had seen Sidney in Paris and seen his villa and everything and his life over there
yeah he must have been quite an idol of the French yeah
I hope someday to meet his son

is there anything else you can tell about the recording sessions or your musical associations in the band? did he actually try to take over and start to run it then when you made the records or did he honor your leadership of it or what did he do? I'm not trying to put you on the spot or anything or don't act self conscious about it I mean don't try to be yeah

well musically he I think he always sort of took over any situation that he was in not because he particularly wanted to or tried to but it was his expression was so powerful that he would just do it oh one other question I was going to say a minute ago
did he ever talk to you about not using a trumpet? I mean did he seem to prefer that or just the fact that he had trouble getting a good trumpet?

yeah he had trouble getting a good trumpet player he didn't like the way most trumpet players played because it got in his way yeah you know he liked working with Muggsy he liked that record he made with Muggsy

well it's funny down here too at the time they had that Esquire concert about 1945 I guess in January of 45 went all over the country they had some rehearsals here I know they had a couple of local bands I think Sharky's band maybe George Lewis or two or three other local bands here played and they told that when Louis Armstrong was leader of this all-star group had been selected by Esquire partly they had gotten votes there at least Sidney came down to play with him and it ended up in quite a little row I remember they quote Louis saying I'm going to have no two leads in my band
Sidney didn't get along with Louis in the later years yeah I guess not he felt that Louis didn't play the way he did in the old days when they played together
yeah
and he was never happy about the 1940 sessions he did with Louis
that Decca session yeah they did
and you remember that Louis Armstrong town hall concert yeah
with Bobby Hackett

no Bobby Hackett and Peanuts well you know Sidney was supposed to be on that no I don't remember that in fact the big thing about that concert was Freddie Robbins was a disc jockey who was running a thing and he had every night in the program for a couple of weeks before the concert he talked about this reunion Sidney Boucher and Louis Armstrong that was the big thing about it
well it never came off

and well what happened was Sidney was going on a subway to the concert and got sick and was just lying there practically unconscious and he rode around the subway for hours people thought he was drunk you know and nobody knew where is Sidney I remember being backstage at this thing and Ernie Anderson and Fred Robbins were saying where is Sidney and they wanted me to go on and play and I wouldn't do it because I you'd be upset too naturally well I was upset too and I also felt I wasn't ready for this I wasn't ready to play with Louis Armstrong and Bobby Hackett and everything which I wasn't at that time you know
yeah that's pretty early when was that? forty-seven
forty-seven
forty-seven yeah you haven't played very long then anyway
but I know Sidney had mixed feelings about playing that concert
I just wondered though in general if he had tried to avoid using a trumpet sometimes so he could be take the lead more himself if he enjoyed it or what do you think? did he ever express it?
I think he enjoyed playing the lead melody yeah
actually soprano sax is near a trumpet and a clarinet almost in some respects

and in some of his records even where he has a trumpet he has the trumpet play a second part and he'll play the melody on soprano yeah he liked to feel like he was leading the whole thing which he could do so well you know

well one other question in regard to your lessons did he ever discuss playing in different registers like you talk about the very high notes or sticking to a low register chorus or any advice on anything of that kind?
he liked to have me play across the registers
yeah yeah
don't stick to one register and then to another you know cover the whole range of the instrument
even in one chorus or one solvon
yeah although actually when he played clarinet he would stick more to one register or the other but this was because he was a little scared about it uncertain yeah

yeah uncertain yeah we have about another two minutes left is there anything that I've been leaving out I've been trying to lead you on with certain questions maybe but is there anything you'd like to talk about other New Orleans musicians as I say we try to specialize in New Orleans history since that's our project but I know you've done a lot of other kinds of work too any other New Orleans musicians in particular that ever impressed you or oh there's many
oh there's many I guess Louis Armstrong impresses me more than any I think I've been playing with with Bobby Hackett now you know
yeah and how long have you been with him now

well I just joined him for this two week engagement but I've been playing off and on with Bobby for five years now and I have tremendous admiration and respect for his playing thanks and his early playing was was more or less inspired by Big Spider back
I was going to say too sorry that Big Spider back

but in the last 10 or 15 years Louis Armstrong is really the predominant influence and his Max Kaminsky had a theory about Bobby's playing which I think is very true he says Bobby Bobby sounds more like early Louis Armstrong Louis Armstrong the way Louis played with Clarence Clarence

Blue Five and behind the blues singers, it's very sensitive cornet type of expression. And he says, I think that's where Bobby got his whole style from. And Bobby loves to play Louis' tunes like Big Butter and Eggman and Someday and Barbecue. He always plays this thing. Cornet chops, silly. I guess he's the only one that still plays that tune.
By the way, did Sidney have any other special numbers that he wrote that you can think of much that maybe didn't get on record?
Yeah, he did. Ghost of the Blues was one of his really good numbers that was written around 1924.
Lawson Seeley's picture on the cover.

Yeah. I made a recording this last year for a classic jazz label of Sidney's compositions. I picked out, I got a hold of all the music I could from Leeds and Clarence Williams and his various publishers and picked out about 10 of his best things.
Yeah.
And he wrote some beautiful things.
Yeah.
Ghost of the Blues is a marvelous tune. Black Stick.
Well, P. Ron recorded that, didn't he? Yeah. That's right.
Yeah.
Yeah. Didn't care much for that P. Ron recording. Still.
And what else? When the Sun Sets Down South.
Yeah.
And, well, there was a lot of things that he composed in his last years, 10 years, which were sort of folk melodies, but very nice little.
Yeah. Some of those things he did over in France. Yeah.
And they became big hits over there.
Yeah. Maybe some of the old Creole numbers. Yeah.
Some of them sold like over a million records.
Well, one other question about how long did you, we keep jumping around, which is all right. It doesn't have to be in special order. How long did you study with Sidney about, would you say?

Well, let's see, I started in the spring of 46. And I studied and lived with Sidney and played with him every night on the job at Ryan's until I went to, let me see, I went to France in February of 1948 with Mesro. Mesro's Panace organized this jazz festival in Nice.
Yeah, I remember.
And, uh, naturally...
And Baby Dogs is over there, and Pops Foster. Yeah.
Naturally, Mes, he wanted Mes to be one of the leaders, and Louie had the other band.
Yeah.

And he wanted Mes to bring Sidney. And, but, but Sidney was playing in Chicago at the time and, and couldn't get out of it. So Sidney told Mes, well, you take Bobby, and he always called me Bobby. So that's when I went over with that band. Mm-hmm. And, uh, then after that, uh, I got married just shortly before I went over there. And, uh, I didn't live with Sidney anymore, you know. I saw him all the time.
Anything to say about Baby Dogs? We've got to have it in a minute.
Oh, yeah. Baby Dogs was marvelous.
I thought so.
God, I thought he was a great drummer.
Yeah.

And I loved playing with him, and he, the way he could make a press roll swing on the drums was just terrific. Yeah. Yeah. That rhythm section was, with, with Sam Price, Pop Foster, and Baby Dogs. That upset, uh, that upset the Armstrong All-Stars.
Yeah.
Uh, we, they all, they naturally would finish the concerts. It was a double bill with the two bands, and, because they were the big, big names, but we gave them an awful rough time.
Yeah, I heard Louie really liked to hear that, too. Yeah. He's really a little bit.

And, uh, Mes and I would play these clarinet duets and everything. Of course, Mes had a thing that he would do, which, what used to get me mad. And he always was having a little read trouble, and, and he would squeak, and he'd always give me a dirty look when he'd squeak. For the, gee, really? He wanted the people to think that I was, you know.
Oh, gee, that's funny. That's pretty good.
But we used to do, uh, all the things that, like, the weary blues, and really the blues, and the things that he'd recorded with Sidney, and I'd take Sidney.

segments.chapter: Early life and New York scene
segments.title: Interview opening and Wilber's birth
segments.summary: Date, place and name are recorded; Wilber was born in New York City in 1928.

segments.chapter: Early life and New York scene
segments.title: First jazz records: Ellington and Armstrong's Hot Five
segments.summary: Wilber recalls Mood Indigo as a toddler and the puzzling first listen to Armstrong Hot Five reissues around 1940 that made him a musician.

segments.chapter: Early life and New York scene
segments.title: Starting clarinet at 13 and growing up in Scarsdale
segments.summary: He began clarinet at 13 with the school band director, played along with records, and met older jazz-collecting friends in Scarsdale.

segments.chapter: Early life and New York scene
segments.title: Young Scarsdale and Westchester bandmates
segments.summary: Wilber names the contemporaries he played with: Wellstead, Glazel, Traeger, Blumberg, Mielke and Fife.

segments.chapter: Early life and New York scene
segments.title: Nick's, 52nd Street and Kelly's Stables as a teenager
segments.summary: Chicago style and Nick's were the big influence; kids sat by the bandstand, and he saw Coleman Hawkins at Kelly's.

segments.chapter: Early life and New York scene
segments.title: Other New York clubs: George's Tavern, Vanguard, Cafe Society
segments.summary: Wilber and the interviewer list clubs and groups from those years, including Teddy Wilson's Cafe Society band.

segments.title: Discovering Bechet and meeting him through Mezzrow
segments.summary: He first knew Bechet from Victor records, heard him live at the Pied Piper, sat in at Ryan's with Mezzrow, and heard of Bechet's planned school.

segments.title: Bechet down and out before the school
segments.summary: The interviewer recalls Bechet's pressing shop in 1939 and his Nick's period; Wilber agrees.

segments.title: Eastman for one term, then returning to study with Bechet
segments.summary: Wilber went to Eastman, missed Bunk Johnson at the Stuyvesant, left after one term and decided to study jazz.

segments.title: Bechet's Brooklyn house and school of music
segments.summary: Bechet's Quincy Street house, his sign, Laura and the Great Dane Butch.

segments.title: First lessons: price, setup and Bechet's enthusiasm
segments.summary: Wilber was the school's only student at $5 a lesson; Bechet was keen to teach his idea of improvisation.

segments.title: Bechet's teaching method: melody then variations
segments.summary: Bechet taught him to play the melody straight then vary it, using popular tunes like Intermezzo and Prisoner of Love, and valued contemporary expression and varied repertoire.

segments.title: Bechet as clarinetist and his teeth trouble
segments.summary: Bechet loved clarinet at home but feared it on jobs; the interviewer recalls his teeth, John Reed and the old-timers' high regard.

segments.title: Stories of Bechet's clarinet prowess
segments.summary: Anecdotes about Bechet outplaying Dodds and Noone, Noone's opinion, and Bechet's best clarinet records for Panassie.

segments.title: Why Bechet did not play more clarinet; his gentle side
segments.summary: Wilber thinks greater speed would have come with more clarinet playing, and notes Bechet's tendency to carry the band and his tender clarinet sound.

segments.title: Albert system clarinets and tone
segments.summary: Discussion of Albert versus Boehm clarinets, large bores, dark tone, and an interviewer's anecdote about a Chicago amateur.

segments.title: Tone differences among Albert and Boehm clarinetists
segments.summary: An interviewer anecdote about a Chicago amateur's embouchure, and Wilber on Albert players like Fazola and Dodds versus Goodman.

segments.title: Bechet's reeds and mouthpieces
segments.summary: Bechet made music with any reed or damaged mouthpiece; anecdotes from Barbarin and Humphrey.

segments.title: Wilber's own reed, mouthpiece and fingering background
segments.summary: Wilber uses a number five Van Doren with a close lay; Bechet gave no fingering advice because Wilber had classical study with Arey and others.

segments.title: Practice advice, tape machine and Bechet's ballet
segments.summary: Bechet advised stopping when tired, recorded himself, composed, played piano and worked on his ballet.

segments.title: Bechet's classical record and Will Marion Cook
segments.summary: The Paris ballet record and Bechet's idealisation of soloing before an orchestra, rooted in his early Will Marion Cook experience.

segments.title: Bechet's lessons: variations, scales, swinging and foot-patting
segments.summary: Bechet focused on variations, phrasing and swing, taught Raggin' the Scale, and said to carry your own rhythm section in your head.

segments.title: Bechet's effect on bands, his tunes, and not reading music
segments.summary: Bechet improved any group, wrote a Johnny Dodds tribute blues, and regretted weak reading.

segments.title: Bechet's stock variations, one-man band record, playing together at Ryan's
segments.summary: Bechet passed on his standard variation choruses; Wilber played twin sopranos with him at Ryan's.

segments.title: Recording with Bechet for Columbia and Circle
segments.summary: Wilber's Wildcats backed Bechet on a Columbia album arranged through Avakian, and made a Circle record; tunes held back from the original album.

segments.title: Bechet's best records and favorites
segments.summary: Wilber picks favorite Bechet records (Cakewalkin' Babies, Indian Summer, Victor sides, Noble Sissle), prefers his earlier tone, and mentions Pagliacci and Song of Songs.

segments.title: Living at Bechet's Brooklyn house and preparing the session
segments.summary: Wilber moved in rent free, rehearsed the Wildcats there, and recalls an earlier nervous Commodore date and the subway trip.

segments.title: Bechet's bad business sense
segments.summary: Bechet bought poor property, spent on equipment and had a failed mink farm.

segments.title: Last time Wilber saw Bechet and Bechet's final years
segments.summary: In 1952-53 Bechet visited with news of a child in France; the interviewer tells of Chicago troubles, stomach illness, and Wilber's regret at never visiting Paris.

segments.title: Bechet taking over sessions and avoiding trumpet
segments.summary: Bechet dominated any situation and disliked most trumpet players getting in his way.

segments.title: Bechet and Louis Armstrong; the missed Town Hall concert
segments.summary: Bechet had strained relations with Armstrong; he fell ill on the subway and missed the 1947 Town Hall reunion concert.

segments.title: Bechet's lead playing and advice on registers
segments.summary: Bechet liked taking the lead melody and told Wilber to cover all registers.

segments.title: Playing with Bobby Hackett and Armstrong's influence
segments.summary: Wilber has played with Hackett for five years; Hackett's style is traced to Armstrong's early playing.

segments.title: Bechet's compositions
segments.summary: Wilber recorded ten Bechet compositions and discusses Ghost of the Blues and the late French folk melodies.

segments.title: Leaving Bechet for the 1948 Nice festival with Mezzrow
segments.summary: He studied with Bechet until February 1948, when Bechet sent him to Nice with Mezzrow's band.

segments.title: Baby Dodds and the Mezzrow rhythm section at Nice
segments.summary: Wilber praises Baby Dodds, the Price-Foster-Dodds rhythm section that unsettled the Armstrong All-Stars, and clarinet duets with Mezzrow.
